title: Signs of Mold in the Attic and What to Do
h1: What Are the Signs of Mold in the Attic?
description: Dark stains on roof sheathing, musty smells, damp insulation and rusty nails are signs of attic mold. Learn what causes it and how it gets fixed for good.
quick_answer: Common signs of attic mold are dark gray, black or green spotting on the underside of the roof deck and rafters, a musty smell in the attic or upstairs rooms, damp or matted insulation, water stains, and rusty nail tips poking through the roof. Mold in an attic almost always means there's a moisture problem that needs fixing too.
body:
Attic mold usually grows quietly for a long time before anyone notices. Most people find it when they go up for storage, during a roof repair, or when a home inspector points it out during a sale. Knowing the early signs helps you catch it while the fix is still simple.

What does attic mold look like?

Mold in attics most often shows up on the underside of the roof sheathing, which is the plywood or boards the roof is nailed to. Look for:

  • Dark gray or black blotches spread across the wood, often on the side of the roof that gets less sun
  • Fuzzy white, green or yellow patches on rafters or sheathing
  • Spotting concentrated around roof vents, bathroom fan ducts or plumbing vents
  • Dark streaks running down from roof penetrations

Not every dark stain is active mold. Old water stains, wood discoloration and soot can look similar. If you're not sure, a professional can tell the difference and test if needed.

What other signs point to mold?

Even if you can't see growth, these clues suggest moisture and possible mold:

  1. A musty, earthy smell when you open the attic hatch, or in upstairs rooms and closets
  2. Damp, clumped or discolored insulation
  3. Rusty nails poking through the roof deck, which means moisture is condensing on the metal
  4. Water stains on ceilings below the attic
  5. Warped or delaminating sheathing
  6. Allergy-like symptoms that seem worse at home, especially if ducts run through the attic

What causes mold in an attic?

Mold needs moisture to grow. In Southern California attics, the moisture usually comes from one of these:

  • Exhaust fans venting into the attic. Bathroom fans that end in the attic instead of outside dump warm, wet air right onto the roof deck. Dryer vents that end in the attic are even worse.
  • Roof leaks. Winter storms can find weak spots around flashing, vents and old roofing.
  • Poor ventilation. Blocked soffit vents or too few vents trap moist air. This is common when insulation gets pushed over the eave vents.
  • Coastal humidity. Near the coast, marine air and cool nights can cause condensation on the roof deck when ventilation is weak.
  • HVAC condensation. AC ducts and equipment in the attic can sweat if they're poorly insulated, and a clogged condensate drain can overflow.
  • Air leaks from the house. Gaps around light fixtures, the attic hatch and plumbing let humid indoor air rise into the attic.

Is attic mold dangerous?

Mold spores can trigger allergies and asthma, and some people are more sensitive than others. Attic mold doesn't always reach the living space, but it can if there are air leaks in the ceiling or if ducts in the attic are leaky. Over time, ongoing moisture can also damage the roof deck and insulation.

Don't scrape or sand moldy wood yourself. Disturbing it sends spores into the air and can spread them through the house.

How is attic mold removed?

A lasting fix has two parts: remove the mold and stop the moisture. A typical job includes:

  1. Finding and correcting the moisture source, such as rerouting a bath fan or fixing ventilation
  2. Removing wet or contaminated insulation
  3. Cleaning and treating affected wood surfaces
  4. Air sealing gaps between the house and the attic
  5. Installing fresh insulation once everything is dry

Roof leaks need a roofer before the cleanup. Our attic cleaning and insulation team handles the removal, sanitizing, air sealing and new insulation. If you're also concerned about mold in the living space or the HVAC system, our indoor air quality services can help.

How can I prevent mold from coming back?

Make sure every bath fan and dryer vent runs all the way outside. Keep eave vents clear of insulation, use your bath fans during and after showers, and have the attic checked after big storms. Fixing air leaks in the ceiling also keeps humid indoor air out of the attic.

It also helps to know where your bath fan ducts end. If you are not sure, have someone run the fan while you look in the attic. You should not feel air blowing into the attic.
faqs: Can I just spray bleach on attic mold?
It's not a good fix. Bleach doesn't soak into wood well, it adds moisture, and it does nothing about the cause. The moisture source has to be fixed, and the mold should be removed with containment.
Does attic mold affect the air in my house?
It can, especially if there are gaps in the ceiling or ductwork in the attic with leaks. Air from the attic can be pulled into the living space.
Will a home inspector flag attic mold?
Often, yes. Inspectors commonly note staining and signs of moisture in the attic. Fixing the cause and cleaning it up before listing a home can help avoid surprises.
Does attic mold mean I need a new roof?
Not usually. Most attic mold comes from ventilation or exhaust issues. If the sheathing has rotted from long-term moisture, some sections may need replacing, which a roofer can assess.
